prompt: What is the half-life of a radioactive isotope?

choices.text: The time it takes for one-half of the isotope to decay
Half the time it takes for all of the isotope to decay
choices.why: Radioactive decay never quite finishes; half-life is the time for half of the sample to decay.

choices.text: The time it takes for the radioactivity to double
choices.why: Radioactivity decreases over time; half-life is the time for half the isotope to decay.

choices.text: Half of the isotope's mass number
choices.why: Half-life is a time, not a mass.

explanation: Half-life is the amount of time it takes for one-half of a radioactive isotope to decay.

prompt: Which statement about the half-life of a specific radioactive isotope is true?

choices.text: It is constant, unaffected by conditions and independent of the initial amount.
It gets shorter as the sample gets smaller.
choices.why: The half-life is the same no matter how much isotope there is.

choices.text: It can be shortened by heating the sample.
choices.why: The half-life is unaffected by conditions.
The half-life stays constant; what halves each time is the amount of isotope.

explanation: The half-life of a specific radioactive isotope is constant; it is unaffected by conditions and is independent of the initial amount of that isotope.

prompt: Which expression gives the amount of a radioactive isotope remaining after n half-lives?

choices.why: That would make the sample grow. Each half-life multiplies the amount by 1/2.
Decay halves the amount each time; it doesn't subtract a fixed quantity.
After 3 half-lives, (1/2)^3 = 1/8 remains, not 1/6.

explanation: amount remaining = initial amount × (1/2)^{n}, where n is the number of half-lives. This expression works even if n is not a whole number.

prompt: A student says that since half of a sample decays in one half-life, all of it will be gone after two half-lives. What is wrong?

choices.text: Each half-life halves what is left, so after two half-lives one-quarter remains.

choices.why: Half remains after one half-life, and half of that, one-quarter, after two.
The second half-life halves the remaining half, leaving 1/4, not zero.

choices.text: Half-lives don't apply after the first one.
choices.why: The half-life is constant; every half-life halves the amount present.

explanation: During each half-life, half of the amount present at its start decays: 1/2 remains after one half-life, 1/4 after two, 1/8 after three.

Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8.04 d. How much of a 50.0 mg sample remains after 20.0 d? Use amount remaining = initial × e^(−0.693 t/t½).
Radon-222 has a half-life of 3.823 d. How much of a 1.00 g sample remains after 10.0 d? Use amount remaining = initial × e^(−0.693 t/t½).
When using amount remaining = initial × e^(−0.693 t/t½), what must be true of t and t½?

choices.text: They must be in the same units of time.
t must always be in seconds and t½ in years.
choices.why: Any time unit works, as long as both are the same, so the units cancel.

choices.text: t must be a whole multiple of t½.
choices.why: This formula is for when t isn't an exact multiple of the half-life.
The ratio t/t½ is only correct if both are in the same units.

explanation: The variables t and t½ should have the same units of time, so that they cancel in the exponent. The time t need not be an exact multiple of half-lives.

prompt: How widely do the half-lives of isotopes vary?

choices.text: From fractions of a microsecond to billions of years
From a few days to a few years
choices.why: Some, like seaborgium-260, last milliseconds; others, like uranium-238, billions of years.

choices.text: They are all about the same
choices.why: Half-lives vary enormously, from fractions of a microsecond to billions of years.
The table alone ranges from 4 ms (seaborgium-260) to 4.47 × 10^9 y (uranium-238).

explanation: Half-lives of isotopes range from fractions of a microsecond to billions of years.

choices.why: 1.26 × 10^9 y is long, but uranium-238's 4.47 × 10^9 y is longer.
7.04 × 10^8 y is shorter than both potassium-40 and uranium-238.
5730 y is by far the shortest of these.

prompt: Most of the radioactivity in the human body comes from which two isotopes?

choices.why: These are present only in tiny amounts, with low activity. Potassium-40 and carbon-14 dominate.
Their activities in the body are small; most comes from potassium-40 and carbon-14.

choices.text: None; the human body isn't radioactive
choices.why: A small portion of certain elements in the body is radioactive, constantly decaying.

explanation: Most of the radioactivity in the human body comes from potassium-40 and carbon-14. We can't live without potassium and carbon, so some radioactivity is unavoidable.

prompt: About how many radioactive decays occur each second in an average human body?

choices.why: The body contains radioactive isotopes like potassium-40 and carbon-14, which decay constantly.
Potassium-40 alone accounts for over 4,000 decays per second; the total is about 8,000.
The activities in the section's table add up to about 8,000 decays per second.

explanation: The activities of the radioactive isotopes in the body add up to about 8,000 decays per second, mostly from potassium-40 and carbon-14.

prompt: Tritium, hydrogen-3, decays with a half-life of 12.3 y. What does it decay into?

choices.text: Helium-3, by emitting a beta particle

choices.why: Tritium decays by beta emission: a neutron becomes a proton, giving helium-3.

choices.text: Helium-4, by emitting an alpha particle
choices.why: Alpha emission would lower the mass number. Tritium undergoes beta decay to helium-3.
Tritium decays from hydrogen-3 to helium-3 by emitting a beta particle.

explanation: Tritium decays from hydrogen-3 to helium-3 by emitting a beta particle: the mass number stays 3, and the atomic number goes from 1 to 2.

prompt: What determines whether a given isotope is radioactive?

choices.text: It is a characteristic of that particular isotope.

choices.why: Radioactivity and half-life are unaffected by conditions like temperature.
Whether an isotope decays doesn't depend on how much of it there is.

choices.text: Whether it is in a compound
choices.why: Radioactivity comes from the nucleus, so it is a property of the isotope itself.

explanation: Whether a given isotope is radioactive is a characteristic of that particular isotope. Some are stable indefinitely; others decay through a characteristic form of emission.
